I am 72 years old now, and my legs aren't what they used to be. I have been farming these 8 mu of land in Quzhou for over 50 years, ever since I was a young man. My father taught me how to read the soil here, and I know what works on the North China Plain. I only finished primary school, but I know my fields.

This year, like most years, I will stick to the wheat-maize rotation. It is the safest choice for a man my age. Cotton pays more when prices are good, but it needs too much labor — spraying pesticides twelve or thirteen times, and the picking is backbreaking work. I cannot bend down like that anymore. My son works in the factory in Handan, so it is mostly just me and my wife now. We need crops that the machines can help with.

For the winter wheat, I sowed about 8 mu last October with improved seeds — I have been using varieties like Jimai 22 or Luyuan 502, which the seed station recommends. They are not traditional old wheat, but they are not fancy hybrids either; they are reliable. Before sowing, I rotary-tilled the soil to break up the stubble from the maize. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer as a base dressing — roughly enough to give about 65 jin of pure nitrogen, 22 jin of phosphorus, and 8 jin of potassium per mu. I also top-dress with urea in the spring when the wheat greens up. I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the wheat survive the cold, and twice more in spring when the grain is filling. I spray pesticides about four times total — twice for insects, once for weeds, and once for fungus when the weather turns humid. I expect around 1,000 jin of wheat per mu if the weather cooperates.

After we harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant summer maize immediately. Everyone here uses no-tillage for maize now — we just drill the seeds directly into the wheat stubble. It saves diesel, saves my strength, and the yields are good. I buy hybrid maize seeds every year, usually Denghai 605 or something similar from the seed shop. These hybrids are expensive, but they give me over 1,100 jin per mu, so it is worth it. For maize, I put down less fertilizer than wheat — about 22 jin of nitrogen, 6 jin of phosphorus, and 6 jin of potassium per mu — because the maize season is shorter and the wheat already took a lot from the soil. I irrigate twice, usually once at jointing and once at filling. I spray about three times: twice for corn borer and other insects, and once for weeds. 

I thought about renting out my land to a family farm, but the rent they offer is too low, and farming is all I know. As long as my health holds, I will keep growing wheat and maize. It puts food on the table and gives me dignity.
